---
title: "The Cache Fill That Resurrects Deleted Data"
description: "Advanced system-design reasoning with formal constraints and a small tested code example."
---

## Interview challenge

A social-profile cache initially holds version 1. Reader R starts a slow database read of version 1. Meanwhile another request updates the profile to version 2, and invalidation removes the old cache entry. Reader R finally finishes and fills the cache with **version 1**, undoing the effect of invalidation.

The hard problem is not cache TTL. It is the **relative ordering of refill and update**.

## Draw the bad timeline

~~~text
t=0: Reader R fetches value v1 from the database (slow)
t=1: Writer W commits v2 to the authoritative store
t=2: Cache invalidation clears v1
t=3: R finishes and writes v1 into empty cache
t=4: Next reader receives stale v1
~~~

An ordinary 'delete cache after DB update' rule is insufficient without considering delayed in-flight fills. This is one reason caching large social graphs is hard; Meta publicly describes such consistency challenges in its cache engineering work.

## Make versions part of the value

Write cache objects as triples $(k,v,x)$ with key $k$, version $v$, and value $x$. A refill or update can replace a cached value only if its version is no older than the current version. The core comparison is

$$
v_{\mathrm{incoming}}\geq v_{\mathrm{stored}}.
$$

If the update changes the value to version 2 before the stale fetch completes, the stale version-1 fill is rejected.

## Actual tested core implementation

~~~ts
const cache = new VersionedCache<string>();
cache.put('user:7',2,'new');
cache.put('user:7',1,'old'); // returns false
cache.get('user:7');         // version 2 and value 'new'
~~~

Use POST /lab/cache and GET /lab/cache?key=user:7. A separate test races a delayed fetch against an incoming newer version.

## The subtle missing case

What if the writer **deletes the entry entirely** instead of writing a version-2 tombstone? The stale reader sees no newer version and may still refill old data. Correct version-aware invalidation often requires retaining a **tombstone/high-watermark version** or checking the authoritative version before accepting a fill.

A completely distributed cache additionally needs coherent version allocation, ordered invalidation or version-checking across regions, and a policy for cache failures. Global linearizability cannot be obtained by changing just one node's Map.

## The high-value follow-up

Which source of truth generates $v$? A local timestamp is risky because clocks can disagree. A monotonic database row version or transaction sequence is generally more reliable. Why not use a constant TTL of 5 seconds? Because 'stale for at most five seconds' is a different guarantee from read-your-writes or no-resurrection.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
v_{k}(t+1)\geq v_{k}(t)
$$

for each accepted write to a **version-aware** cache, including invalidations represented by tombstones. This monotonic-version invariant prevents stale overwrites, but does not automatically enforce global read linearizability.

**Engineering reference:** Meta Engineering, [Cache made consistent](https://engineering.fb.com/2022/06/08/core-infra/cache-made-consistent/) and [TAO: The power of the graph](https://engineering.fb.com/2013/06/25/core-infra/tao-the-power-of-the-graph/).
